series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 1/3] mm: vmscan: allow writeout of swapcache folios without anon mappings
series_items.patch_summary: This patch allows the writeout of swapcache folios without anonymous mappings, enabling reclaim to write out dirty pages in swapcache even if they don't have an anonymous mapping. This is necessary because pageout() previously rejected these pages before they could be written out using the existing swap writeout path. The change affects how the filesystem checks for valid mappings and allows swapcache folios to bypass certain checks.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 2/3] mm/swap: publish cluster tables after reacquiring allocator locks
series_items.patch_summary: This patch addresses a memory pressure scenario where the swap cluster population table is published while its locks are dropped, allowing it to be consumed and freed by another allocator before the original allocator resumes. To prevent this, the patch ensures that the cluster tables are kept private until they are fully restored after reacquiring all allocator locks. This approach maintains the integrity of the cluster allocation process and prevents potential data corruption or inconsistencies.

series_items.patch_summary: This patch series addresses a bug in the swap cluster relocation logic, where a stale reclaimer can free a tableless cluster while another allocator is still populating its table. patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH] mm: mglru: splice all generations when reparenting a memcg

version_history.subject: [PATCH] mm: mglru: splice all generations when reparenting a memcg

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch fixes a list_del corruption issue in the Linux kernel's memory management system (mm) by splicing all generations of MGLRU lists when reparenting a memcg (memory control group). The problem occurs when a memcg goes offline and its MGLRU lists are moved to the parent, but only certain generations are moved. This can lead to a folio being left on a freed memcg, causing a use-after-free error. To fix this, the patch moves all MAX_NR_GENS lists, not just those from min_seq to max_seq, ensuring that all folios are properly reparented and avoiding the corruption issue.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 1/2] x86/lib: Keep the scalar memcpy() count in RCX
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the x86 implementation of the memcpy function to store the loop count in the RCX register instead of RDX, and uses RDX as a temporary for small-copy data. This change is made to prepare for the ERMS size check to use RDX as scratch while preserving the REP MOVSB count in RCX. The patch does not introduce any functional changes.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 2/2] x86/lib: Use REP MOVSB for large memcpy() on ERMS CPUs without FSRM
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the x86 memcpy() function to use REP MOVSB for large memory copies on ERMS CPUs without FSRM, improving performance by up to 66.8% in certain scenarios. The change involves adding an alternative instruction sequence that uses REP MOVSB when the copy size is 2048 bytes or larger, while keeping the scalar loop for smaller copies. This approach takes into account the specific characteristics of ERMS CPUs and their lack of FSRM support.

review_comments.author: Peter Zijlstra
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Peter Zijlstra noted that the patches introduce a divergence between memcpy and rep_movs_alternative, suggesting it would be beneficial to merge these two functions for consistency.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Wed, Nov 11, 2026 at 05:20:53AM -0800, Usama Arif wrote:
> Since commit 68674f94ffc9 ("x86: don't use REP_GOOD or ERMS for small
> memory copies"), memcpy() uses REP MOVSB only on FSRM CPUs, so ERMS CPUs
> without FSRM, such as Skylake and Cooper Lake, copy every size with
> the scalar loop. Large copies matter there: in Meta's x86 fleet, about a
> third of the time in memcpy_orig() is btrfs zstd decompression copying
> pages into and out of zstd's buffers.
> 
> Use REP MOVSB from 2048 bytes on ERMS CPUs. On a 1.4 GHz Cooper Lake, an
> aligned, cache-hot 4 KiB memcpy() then takes 66.8% less time (123.3 ns
> instead of 371.6 ns). In a single-vCPU guest, reading a synthetic
> 512 MiB btrfs zstd file takes 14.8% less time (median of five kernel
> pairs). Smaller copies keep the scalar loop: using REP MOVSB from
> 32 bytes made 32/64/128/256-byte copies
> 111.8%/68.0%/63.2%/15.6% slower.
> 
> Prepare the return value and RCX count before the FSRM alternative. On
> FSRM CPUs, REP MOVSB replaces the jump to memcpy_orig(), followed by a
> RET in ordinary text. ITS then selects return handling using the RET's
> execution address.
> 
> For ERMS CPUs, shift the scratch copy of the length in RDX after the
> 32-byte check. RCX already holds the count, so large copies need no
> reload. Copies below 32 bytes skip the check, which is a single NOP
> without ERMS.

So no real objection to these patches from me.

However, it did remind me of something I have on the TODO list for a
rainy afternoon, namely merge memcpy and rep_movs_alternative.

It makes very little sense to me that we have two (divergent) copies of
what is basically the same thing.

review_comments.summary: Reviewer noted that the patch's approach of modifying the memcpy() function call for large copies may not be effective, as many memcpy() calls are not actual function calls at the C level and compilers can already optimize small memcpy() calls into loads and stores. Linus suggested that a better optimization would be to modify the calling convention to use 'rep movs' instead of a function call, which could then be replaced with 'rep movsb'.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Fri, 13 Nov 2026 at 08:03, David Laight <david.laight.linux@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I was thinking more of something like:
> (written in the email so untested)
>
> static always_inline void *memcpy(void *dst, const void *src, size_t len)

The problem with this approach two-fold:

 - many memcpy() calls aren't actually memcpy() calls on a C level

 - many memcpy() that *are* calls on a C level should never be calls
in the generated code

That first case is for things like structure copies etc. And it's
common, and it's important, although for the kernel it's usually a
non-issue because it's *typicay* a small constant-sized copy, which
brings us to the second case...

The second case is hugely important. The compiler needs to turn small
memcpy() calls into just loads and stores. Calling "memcpy()" for a
known 64-byte copy is hugely inefficient.

We used to - long ago - do that "constant small sizes" thing by hand.
It was a huge pain. We now rely on the compiler to do it.

End result: we must *not* hide 'memcpy()' from the compiler for
performance reasons, and we cannot catch all cases anyway because the
compiler generates implicit memcpy calls.

This is why I really wish we had the compiler just generate a
different sequence for 'call memcpy'. One that used a different
callign convention - preferably just the 'rep movs' one so that we
could just rewrite the call with 'rep movsb' in place.

Without compiler support, we're kind of screwed.

You misunderstand.

Avoiding call-clobbered registers means that the caller has more

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series optimizes the x86 memcpy() function for ERMS CPUs without FSRM by using REP MOVSB for large copies (2048 bytes and larger). The approach taken is to split the changes into two patches: one that prepares the scalar register allocation, and another that adds the ERMS size check and adopts Linus's FSRM entry layout. This allows REP MOVSB to replace the existing jump to memcpy_orig(), keeping RET in ordinary text. The patch also addresses issues related to return handling and register reloads.

> Since commit 68674f94ffc9 ("x86: don't use REP_GOOD or ERMS for small
> memory copies"), memcpy() uses REP MOVSB only on FSRM CPUs, so ERMS CPUs
> without FSRM, such as Skylake and Cooper Lake, copy every size with
> the scalar loop. Large copies matter there: in Meta's x86 fleet, about a
> third of the time in memcpy_orig() is btrfs zstd decompression copying
> pages into and out of zstd's buffers.
> 
> Use REP MOVSB from 2048 bytes on ERMS CPUs. On a 1.4 GHz Cooper Lake, an
> aligned, cache-hot 4 KiB memcpy() then takes 66.8% less time (123.3 ns
> instead of 371.6 ns). In a single-vCPU guest, reading a synthetic
> 512 MiB btrfs zstd file takes 14.8% less time (median of five kernel
> pairs). Smaller copies keep the scalar loop: using REP MOVSB from
> 32 bytes made 32/64/128/256-byte copies
> 111.8%/68.0%/63.2%/15.6% slower.
>

> FSRM CPUs, REP MOVSB replaces the jump to memcpy_orig(), followed by a
> RET in ordinary text. ITS then selects return handling using the RET's
> execution address.

> 32-byte check. RCX already holds the count, so large copies need no
> reload. Copies below 32 bytes skip the check, which is a single NOP
> without ERMS.

rainy afternoon, namely merge memcpy and rep_movs_alternative.

review_comments.summary: Reviewer Linus Torvalds expressed concerns that hiding the 'memcpy()' function from the compiler could lead to performance issues, particularly for small copies, and suggested that the compiler should generate a different sequence for 'call memcpy' using a different calling convention.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Fri, 13 Nov 2026 at 08:03, David Laight <david.laight.linux@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I was thinking more of something like:
> (written in the email so untested)
>
> static always_inline void *memcpy(void *dst, const void *src, size_t len)

The problem with this approach two-fold:

 - many memcpy() calls aren't actually memcpy() calls on a C level

 - many memcpy() that *are* calls on a C level should never be calls
in the generated code

That first case is for things like structure copies etc. And it's
common, and it's important, although for the kernel it's usually a
non-issue because it's *typicay* a small constant-sized copy, which
brings us to the second case...

The second case is hugely important. The compiler needs to turn small
memcpy() calls into just loads and stores. Calling "memcpy()" for a
known 64-byte copy is hugely inefficient.

We used to - long ago - do that "constant small sizes" thing by hand.
It was a huge pain. We now rely on the compiler to do it.

End result: we must *not* hide 'memcpy()' from the compiler for
performance reasons, and we cannot catch all cases anyway because the
compiler generates implicit memcpy calls.

This is why I really wish we had the compiler just generate a
different sequence for 'call memcpy'. One that used a different
callign convention - preferably just the 'rep movs' one so that we
could just rewrite the call with 'rep movsb' in place.

Without compiler support, we're kind of screwed.

              Linus

              Linus

On Sat, 14 Nov 2026 at 14:45, David Laight <david.laight.linux@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Otherwise you'll need to spill to stack for even a simple byte copy loop.

I think the optimization should be for the inline case.

Once you do a call, having a couple of push/pop instructions in the
target is a complete no-op.

But having extra registers free could help at the call-site, and if
the 'rep movs' is inlined you only modify rcx/rsi/rdi. I think the
calling convention should mirror that.

             Linus

---

On Sun, 15 Nov 2026 at 04:42, David Laight <david.laight.linux@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> > But having extra registers free could help at the call-site,
>
> There isn't much you can put at the call site instead of a 5 byte call.

You misunderstand.

Avoiding call-clobbered registers means that the caller has more
registers live and can do better code generation.

Making the calling convention clobber registers that aren't useful is
*bad*. And if you do a loop - which you know is either large or
unknown size - and take the I$ hit, adding a couple of push/pop
instructions really doesn't hurt AT ALL.

It has nothing to do with the 5-byte "'call' or 'rep movsb'" instruction.

(And I realize that 'rep movsb' is only two bytes. You'd add a 3-byte
nop or harmless prefixes to it depending on which decodes better)

             Linus
